title: Knowledge Check 5: Lessons 33-40
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 33-40 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Hands on with one framework, a real agent that does real work", what does the Runner own in the OpenAI Agents SDK?
options: The loop: it calls the model, inspects the output, runs any tool calls the model requests, feeds the results back, and repeats until the model returns a final answer
Only the retry logic for failed API calls
The persistence of conversation history across turns
The scoring of the agent's outputs against a golden set
questions.explanation: The lesson defines the Runner as owning the reason-act-observe loop that you built by hand earlier, and says every other primitive builds on that one loop rather than replacing it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an input guardrail in the lesson's terms?
options: It validates the model's final answer before the user sees it
It checks the incoming user message and raises a tripwire exception, failing fast before the expensive model spends tokens or a tool touches a system it should not
It redacts personal data from tool results
It caps how many tool calls a single run may make
questions.explanation: The lesson says an input guardrail runs against the incoming user message, usually in parallel with the main agent, and its job is to fail fast on off-scope or hostile requests.

questions.question: Why does the lesson grow the ticket triager into a ticket resolver?
options: Because routing accuracy is the hardest part of the agent loop
Because the framework cannot produce structured output for a classifier
Because classifying a ticket and stopping leaves the real effort, gathering context, applying policy, and drafting a reply, to a person
Because classification requires a larger model than resolution does
questions.explanation: The lesson says classification alone is not work a human would hand an agent, so the resolver reads the issue, looks up the account and order, checks the refund policy, and drafts a reply a contact center could actually send.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Agent UX: streaming output, progress indicators, and when users need to see the loop", what feedback should an agent UI give once a run passes the ten-second attention limit?
options: A percentage-done bar, even when the number of remaining steps is unknown
A real progress indicator that tells the user what to expect, plus a way to interrupt the run
No feedback at all, because agent latency is unavoidable
The model's raw chain-of-thought, streamed so the wait feels productive
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the response-time bands: past ten seconds the user's attention is gone, so they need a progress indicator that says what to expect and a way to interrupt.

questions.question: The lesson says an agent UI runs two distinct signals and that conflating them is the most common mistake. Which statement matches that guidance?
options: Streaming the answer is enough; the work should stay hidden
Reporting progress on the work makes streaming the answer unnecessary
Stream the answer for tolerability and report the work for reassurance, because they do different jobs
Both signals should be rendered at token granularity so a step list can be built from tokens
questions.explanation: The lesson's core mental model is that the answer streams at token granularity to make the wait tolerable, while the work is reported per completed item to reassure the user, and doing only one of the two produces a broken experience.

questions.question: How does the lesson say you should build a progress step list from an agent framework's event stream?
options: Render raw tool arguments and private reasoning as the visible steps
Mark the run done as soon as the last visible token lands
Fake a percentage when the loop has no fixed step count
Use per-item events such as tool_called and tool_output, because a tool call is a unit a human can understand while a token is not
questions.explanation: The lesson points to per-item stream events like tool_called, tool_output, and message_output_created as the level to render a step list from, and warns against showing raw tool JSON or reasoning.

questions.question: Per the lesson "RAG at Scale: Ingestion Pipelines, Refresh, Versioning, and Deletion", what framing makes the write side of RAG click?
options: Treat your embeddings as a materialized view over your source data: derived, expensive to compute, written once, queried often, and assumed correct downstream
Treat the index as a nightly backup of the source system
Treat documents as immutable once they have been embedded
Treat retrieval as a pure cache with no freshness requirement
questions.explanation: The lesson borrows the materialized-view framing from data warehousing and says that once you see embeddings that way, the questions about source of truth, freshness, backfill, and deletes become obvious.

questions.question: The lesson names a failure mode where the vectors stay frozen while the world keeps moving. What is it called?
options: Hallucination drift
The index is a photograph: vectors are frozen from the moment of embedding, so the assistant answers confidently from a policy that has since changed
Vector collapse
Embedding decay
questions.explanation: The lesson uses the photograph framing to explain that staleness degrades retrieval quality silently and confidently, because a stale chunk looks identical to a current one.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about deletion in a RAG system?
options: Deleting content in the source system automatically removes the vectors
Deletion is unnecessary as long as refresh runs often enough
A vector database is separate from the source system, so a deletion does not propagate on its own and must be treated as a first-class operation in the pipeline
Deletion only matters for text documents, never for structured records
questions.explanation: The lesson defines deletion as removing content from retrieval when the source removes it or access is revoked, and says the separation between vector store and source means the pipeline must handle it explicitly.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Testing Agents: Unit Tests for Tools, Integration Tests, and Regression Evals", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: Test the properties of outputs rather than exact outputs, test the deterministic layers as ordinary software, and score the fuzzy end with an evaluator kept honest by a frozen baseline
Assert exact output strings and fail the build whenever they change
Skip automated testing because agent output is stochastic
Rely on manual review of every run before release
questions.explanation: The lesson says the model is a moving target, so you wrap it in checks you can pin down and add an evaluator layer for the fuzzy end, turning is it ready to ship into a number with a threshold.

questions.question: How does the lesson define an integration test for an agent?
options: A test that stubs the model and asserts on a prompt string
A test that runs the whole agent loop against controlled tool side effects, asserting the sequence and outcome, such as the right tool called with the right arguments in the right order
A test that scores real output with an LLM judge against a golden set
A test that measures cost per request under load
questions.explanation: The lesson defines integration tests as running the whole loop with mocked tools that return fixed data, so the assertion is on tool selection, argument formation, ordering, and that nothing destructive happened.

questions.question: The lesson says teams sink their testing effort by leading with the expensive layer. What structure does it recommend instead?
options: Run LLM-as-judge evaluations on every commit
Replace unit tests with live production experiments
A costed pyramid: cheap deterministic assertions on every pull request, model-based evaluation nightly or before release, and live experiments only after the lower layers pass
Test only in production and roll back on failure
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the pyramid explicitly, warning that wiring up expensive eval judges on every commit leads teams to quietly stop running them.

questions.question: Per the lesson "CI/CD for Agents: Prompt Versioning, Model Registries, and Canary Releases", why does an agent break the assumptions conventional CI/CD is built on?
options: Its behavior is shaped by the code, the model, the prompts, and the retrieved data, and each of those can change independently of the codebase
Its test suites are too slow to run on every commit
Its behavior is fully determined by code, so versioning adds no value
Its dependencies cannot be pinned inside a build artifact
questions.explanation: The lesson opens by naming the three ways an agent breaks the code-determines-behavior assumption: the model, the prompts, and the retrieved data can each change without any application code changing.

questions.question: A team wants to canary a new prompt revision for a conversational support agent. Which practice does the lesson prescribe?
options: Compare the canary against a historical baseline from an earlier month
Run both versions concurrently, compare their metrics against each other, and make rollback a routing change rather than a redeploy
Route each request independently so traffic mixes freely between versions
Skip quality scoring until the canary has reached full traffic
questions.explanation: The lesson says the canary and the stable version run concurrently and are compared with each other, that rollback is an instant routing change, and that conversational agents must be routed by session rather than by request.

questions.question: Why does the lesson treat a model registry as necessary when the agent calls an external model through an API?
options: It stores the model weights so the team owns the model outright
It replaces evaluation datasets as the evidence of quality
You do not own the model and providers move versions under you, so the registry is the system of record for which version produced a given output
It automatically rewrites prompts when quality drifts
questions.explanation: The lesson describes this blindness directly: a model that answered acceptably in June may behave differently later without notice, so the registry pins and records the exact version behind any output.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Observability at Scale: Metrics, Alerts, Cost Dashboards, and SLOs", what is the one idea to carry out?
options: At scale, observability is a decision system rather than a viewing window: metrics detect change, alerts route it, dashboards make the trend visible, and SLOs set the threshold between a tolerated change and a page
Every trace should still be read by a human so wrong answers are caught early
Only operational metrics matter, because quality is caught by evals
SLOs make alerts unnecessary once they are defined
questions.explanation: The lesson states that the trace stops being the primary interface at scale and becomes the evidence you open after a metric or alert tells you where to look.

questions.question: The lesson groups agent metrics into three categories that catch different failure modes. Which set does it name?
options: Latency, throughput, and saturation
Operational, economic, and quality proxy metrics
Trace, span, and log metrics
Input, output, and cache metrics
questions.explanation: The lesson separates operational metrics about whether the system works, economic metrics about what it costs, and quality proxy metrics like retry and refusal rate that lead a bad answer before an eval runs.

questions.question: Why does the lesson say uptime is not the same as reliability for an agent?
options: Because agents cannot be monitored with standard observability tools
Because agent latency thresholds are different from a web service's
Because an agent can be fast, up, and returning a 200 while it misunderstands intent, retrieves the wrong context, calls the wrong tool, or leaks sensitive data
Because agents do not emit an error rate metric
questions.explanation: The lesson contrasts a traditional service that fails by being slow, down, or erroring with an agent that can be perfectly healthy operationally while producing the wrong answer or leaking data.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Production Troubleshooting: Debugging Loops, Bad Tools, and Context Bloat", what triage order should you follow on one failing trace?
options: Check for repetition of the same tool call with the same arguments first, then whether a tool result matches its stated success, then whether input tokens are climbing turn over turn
Restart the service, check infrastructure metrics, then read traces
Inspect context length first, then prompt wording, then tool schemas
Compare against a historical baseline before opening any trace
questions.explanation: The lesson gives exactly this order: repetition in the trace means a loop, a tool result that does not match its stated success means a bad tool, and token counts climbing turn over turn mean context bloat.

questions.question: How does the lesson define a loop?
options: Any agent that calls a tool more than once during a run
The same decision made twice without new information arriving between the two
Any run that exceeds its framework step cap
Any run that retries after a tool returns an error
questions.explanation: The lesson uses that definition to exclude things people mislabel: three different search queries are not a loop, while calling the same order-status tool eight times with the same argument is.

questions.question: What does the lesson say about a framework step cap such as max_turns or recursion_limit?
options: It is a diagnosis of the root cause
It prevents loops by forcing new information into the context
It is a seatbelt rather than a diagnosis, and reading the error precisely tells you which of two situations you are in
It should be raised or removed in production so complex tasks can finish
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the shipped defaults from two frameworks and says the step cap is a seatbelt, with the error itself telling you which situation you are actually in.

questions.question: Per the lesson "Case Study: Customer Support Agent Architecture", what is the one idea to carry out about a support agent?
options: A support agent is mostly a routing problem with a retrieval step in the middle and a hard cap on what it is allowed to do
A support agent should be a free-running agent that decides everything dynamically
Support automation only works when every case is fully automated end to end
Reasoning quality, not architecture, decides most support outcomes
questions.explanation: The lesson states that a support agent is mostly a routing problem with a retrieval step in the middle and a hard limit on what it may do, and that most production failures come from getting one of those three wrong.

questions.question: Following the lesson's workflow-versus-agent guidance, how should the common, well-defined support intents be handled?
options: Hand the whole conversation to a free-running agent so it can adapt to anything
Route a classified intent into a constrained, mostly predetermined path, reserving open-ended agent behavior for the long tail
Build a separate free-running agent per intent and let each choose its own tools
Skip routing entirely and let retrieval decide the path
questions.explanation: The lesson applies Anthropic's guidance: start with the simplest solution and only add complexity when needed, so common intents get predictable workflow paths while the open-ended agent is reserved for weird, unstructured requests.

questions.question: The lesson's setup states the goal for the support agent. Which goal does it state?
options: Fully automate every support case so no human is involved
Answer from the model's own knowledge to avoid retrieval cost
Resolve the easy cases end to end and hand the hard ones to a person with full context
Route every case to a human and have the agent draft suggestions only
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that the goal is not full automation of everything: the agent resolves the easy cases end to end and escalates the hard ones to a person with full context.
